paragraphs.text: Dystonia-25 is an autosomal dominant form of primary torsion dystonia. Onset is usually in adulthood but can range from childhood to late adulthood. The disorder mainly begins in the neck as cervical dystonia. In over half of patients it spreads to other muscles, especially the cranial and facial muscles, and speech is often affected (Fuchs et al., 2013).

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) studied 28 carriers of GNAL mutations with definite dystonia from 8 families. Family P was of mixed Russian and Swiss Mennonite ancestry, and the other families were Caucasians of mixed European origin. Mean age at onset was 31.3 years (range, 7 to 54 years). Onset was in the neck in 82% of patients, and 93% had neck involvement at final examination. Only 46% still had focal dystonia at last examination, 57% had cranial involvement, and 44% had speech involvement. No patient had onset in the arm, and only 32% eventually had arm involvement. The authors noted that this distinguished the GNAL phenotype from DYT6. Overall, the phenotype was mainly cervical dystonia, with a fairly broad range of onset ages and spread to other muscles, especially facial muscles, in over half of patients.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing in 2 families with autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia (families P and D1). They found heterozygous mutations in the GNAL gene: a nonsense mutation (S293X) in family P and a missense mutation (V137M) in family D1. Both mutations segregated with the disease. Sanger sequencing of GNAL in 39 additional multiplex families with primary torsion dystonia found 6 more heterozygous mutations (19%). These families were of mixed European origin and negative for DYT1 and DYT6 mutations. The 6 mutations were E155K, an S95fs frameshift, an R198fs frameshift, a splice site mutation (c.274-5T-C), R21X, and an in-frame deletion of pro102 to val104. Segregation analysis confirmed that the mutations were transmitted with the disease. None of the variants were present in dbSNP135, in about 3,500 European exomes, or in 572 control chromosomes. Fuchs et al. (2013) used a BRET assay in HEK293 cells to measure coupling of Galpha-olf to the dopamine D1 receptor (D1R). The S293X mutant supported no D1R-driven responses. The missense mutants E155K and V137M gave intermediate results, consistent with impaired association with Gbeta-gamma subunits. A V16F variant, found in 1 control, behaved like wildtype. The authors concluded that the findings suggested loss of function.

paragraphs.text: In medium spiny neurons, Galpha-olf couples D1R and the adenosine A2A receptor (A2AR) to activation of adenylyl cyclase type 5. Fuchs et al. (2013) proposed that GNAL mutations point to primary abnormalities of D1R and/or A2AR transmission as a possible cause of dystonia. Unlike mutations causing dopa-responsive dystonia, this would place the primary defect postsynaptically, in striatal dopaminoceptive neurons and/or cholinergic interneurons.

paragraphs.text: Bressman et al. (1994) examined 53 individuals from 4 generations of a non-Jewish North American family with adult-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia. Seven family members were affected, with a mean age at onset of 28.4 years (range, 7 to 50 years). In 6 of the 7, the neck was affected first. All 7 developed cervical dystonia, and 5 had dysarthria or dysphonia. Linkage data excluded the DYT1 region on chromosome 9q34. The authors concluded that a gene other than DYT1 is responsible for some cases of adult cervical-onset dystonia.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) used exome sequencing to study family D1, a family of mixed European origin with autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia. In affected members they found a heterozygous c.409G-A transition in the GNAL gene, resulting in a val137-to-met (V137M) substitution. The mutation segregated with the disease in the family and was not found in 572 control chromosomes. Seven carriers were affected. Six had segmental dystonia beginning in the neck between 19 and 50 years of age. The proband had dystonia beginning in the legs at age 7 years, and it became generalized. In a BRET assay of coupling to the dopamine D1 receptor, the V137M mutant gave intermediate results, consistent with impaired association with Gbeta-gamma subunits.

paragraphs.text: In the proband of family N, a man of mixed European origin with focal neck dystonia beginning at age 20 years, Fuchs et al. (2013) found a heterozygous 9-bp deletion (c.304_312delCCTCCAGTT) in the GNAL gene. The deletion results in the in-frame loss of residues pro102 to val104. The variant was not found in dbSNP135, in about 3,500 European exomes, or in 572 control chromosomes.
